newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Congo university in disarray after Mobutu years.
newsitem.headline: Congo university in disarray after Mobutu years.

text.p: The cocks crowed and the chickens pecked for food in the red dust of Africa by the door of the hall where economist Laby Piana of Lubumbashi University gave his first lecture of the post-Mobutu era.

Several hundred sophomore students, packed like sardines onto benches under the tin roof of the bungalow, took notes in the half-light as he explained his view of the dispute that has brought most of the university to a standstill.

The new rulers of the country, renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo after 26 years as Zaire, have cut tuition fees to $60 a year from $100. In response most of the professors and lecturers have come out on strike over reduced salaries.

The dispute illustrates the decline of state institutions under deposed president Mobutu Sese Seko and the massive task of reconstruction which faces the ruling Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of the Congo (AFDL).

"Most of the students have parents who haven't been paid for two or three years and then the university asks them to pay tuition fees. It's just not fair," said Prosper Ngoy Nday, one of the first-year economics students.
"It's not the time to go on strike...We have to make sacrifices too," agreed Piana, one of the few faculty members willing to keep working on the lower salaries.
YEARS OF NEGLECT
This latest hitch in higher education in this southeastern mining city is just the tip of the iceberg at a university which has seen little investment since it opened in the 1960s.

More then 10,000 students squeeze into facilities built for 1,000. The entire campus has four computers, hidden away in one of the science faculties, and the library would hardly do justice to a small-town secondary school in Europe or North America.
"Just look at this room. This isn't an auditorium, it's a hangar," said Tshungu Muganza, pointing to the shabby room where Piana has been lecturing.
But the students, fluent in French and highly politicised, have other concerns beyond the mere material.
They say that the political culture of the Mobutu government brought corruption, croneyism, repression and incompetence onto the university campus.

They recall a massacre of students at Lubumbashi University in 1991, when Mobutu's soldiers took revenge for an incident in which students beat up a prominent general's daughter because she argued against their decision to stage a protest.
"The children of big people spent all year in (the capital) Kinshasa and at the end of the year they passed their exams without even sitting them. That was the system," said Nday.
"Throughout the education system they taught us Mobutu and Mobutuism. We used to sing and dance for Mobutu. If you refused, they would cut off your head," he added.
UNCERTAINTY ABOUT THE FUTURE

Hopes are high that a new government under former rebel leader Laurent Kabila will put things right but they do not expect instant solutions and even at this early stage they are on the alert for signs that the AFDL will betray their trust.
"There's great hope that the university will change for the better and I'm optimistic," said student Daddy Kasungo. "But it won't be immediate. We'll have to wait two or three years."
"We're watching the AFDL and we will see how they work. We have a certain trust," he added.
But Mubiayi Kankunku, another student, already has reservations about the new authorities, less than two months after the rebels took control of Lubumbashi.
"We've noticed that what you need to succeed is an AFDL diploma, not a university degree. We're worried we will have to attend political courses and we don't need that," he said.

The AFDL, following a pattern set by Uganda's National Resistance Movement in the 1980s, believes that after decades of bad government the people need radical reeducation through seminars on subjects such as democracy and human rights.
"That kind of thing may be okay for the people in the villages or in the market place but not for us," said Mubiayi.
Patrick Kalume has another concern, shared by many others in the southern province of Katanga -- the high proportion of people of Rwandan Tutsi origin in Kabila's entourage.
"Kabila has brought many Rwandans with him and we don't want to work with them. We want to work with Zaireans and we want these Rwandans to all go home," he said.
